concept.name: Dry-up volume
concept.definition: A pronounced contraction of volume during a pullback or a test of a prior extreme, interpreted in Wyckoff methodology as a drying up of pressure from the side being tested: secondary tests and springs are expected to occur on markedly lower volume than the climax that preceded them.
concept.intuition: If price revisits a level and hardly anyone trades, the side that drove it there last time may have run out of ammunition.
concept.mechanics: Volume on a reaction or retest is compared with the volume of the prior move in the same direction; a dry-up shows volume falling well below both the climax volume and the recent average while price holds the level, suggesting supply (or demand) is spent.
concept.failure_modes: Low volume can reflect simple disinterest, holiday conditions, or a pre-news lull rather than exhausted supply, and a dry-up offers no protection when genuinely new information enters the market.
concept.misconceptions: A low-volume pullback is not automatically bullish or bearish; it acquires meaning only relative to a prior high-volume event at the same location.
concept.example: After a selling climax on 2M shares, the retest of the low two weeks later trades only 400K shares and closes unchanged — a dry-up suggesting the selling supply is exhausted.
